about.title: About Understanding Outbreaks
chain.select_columns: The needed columns were read from the source file without changing values.
chain.iso2_to_iso3: Two-letter country codes were converted to ISO 3166 three-letter codes.
chain.week_end_to_week_start: Weeks labelled by their last day were relabelled by their first day (Monday).
chain.sum_daily_to_iso_week: Daily values were added up into ISO weeks (Monday to Sunday). An unfinished final week was left out.
chain.sum_surveillance_systems: Values from sentinel, non-sentinel and unspecified surveillance systems were added together. The separate series remain available.
chain.dengue_annual_mixed: One yearly value per country was chosen: a yearly record where the source has one, otherwise the sum of 12 monthly or at least 52 weekly records, using the broadest case definition available.
method.window_rate: Reported values in the most recent complete periods were added up and divided by population (or by samples tested, for influenza).
method.period_rate: The reported value for one period was divided by population (or by samples tested, for influenza).
method.sum_reporting_countries: Values were added across all countries that reported to the source in each period.
method.group_by_disease_place_gap: Notices about the same disease and overlapping places, published no more than 120 days apart, were grouped into one event.
method.active_rank: Events were ordered by a documented score combining recency, reported counts, number of countries and source type.
method.rolling_baseline_c2: A period is flagged when its reported count is well above the mean of that place’s own recent baseline (mean plus three standard deviations, with safeguards).
method.reconcile_pairwise: Values from different sources for the same place, period, metric and definition were compared; nothing was merged.
method.population_density: Population (World Bank) was divided by land area (GeoNames).
method.weekly_changes: New events, changes between the two most recent complete periods, new flags and corrections were listed for the past seven days.
method.quality_metrics: Freshness, completeness, revision rate and lag were computed from the pipeline’s own records.
method.revision_recording: Each pipeline run stored every value that was new or different from the previous snapshot.
method.gazetteer_match: Place names in the notice were matched against this project’s own country, region and city tables.
cite.how.p1: Cite the original source for any number you use, and this site as the place you obtained it. Every trace panel and export contains a suggested citation with the snapshot id, so that readers can see exactly the data you saw.
cite.how.p2: Snapshots are immutable. A link with a snapshot parameter reproduces the view, its sources and its numbers as they were published on that date.
quality.notes.p1: Completeness is the share of countries that have ever reported to a source that are present in its most recent complete periods. Revision rate is the share of published values that later changed. Both need several snapshots before they mean much.
quality.notes.p2: A source is marked “not updated recently” when its latest period is older than twice its expected cadence plus two weeks. When a source fails validation, the last good data stays live and a maintainer is notified through a public issue.
methodology.scope.title: What this site is and is not
methodology.scope.p1: Understanding Outbreaks collects official public reports, keeps a record of where each value came from, and explains how to read them. It does not run surveillance, detect outbreaks, issue alerts, forecast, or give medical advice.
methodology.scope.p2: Simulations in “Learn and simulate” are teaching tools. They are never fitted to the reported data and never describe a real current outbreak.
methodology.provenance.title: Sources and provenance
methodology.provenance.p1: Every source is defined once in a registry with its publisher, link, license, citation and update cadence. Every value carries the id of its source, a link to the dataset or query it came from, a reference to its place in the raw file, the hash of that raw file, when it was retrieved, the snapshot it was published in, and the ordered list of transformations applied.
methodology.provenance.p2: Each item has exactly one origin type: source-reported, site-derived, user-supplied or simulated. Raw files are archived and linked where the source’s license allows redistribution; otherwise only the hash, metadata and link are kept, and the trace panel says so.
methodology.normalization.title: Normalization and rates
methodology.normalization.p1: Countries use ISO 3166 codes. Weeks start on Monday (ISO weeks); months and years start on their first day. Values are kept exactly as published; negative values published by a source as retrospective corrections are kept and flagged.
methodology.normalization.p2: Rates are reported values divided by the World Bank’s most recent total population for the country, times 100,000. One reference population year is used for the whole series, which slightly misstates rates for years far from it. Influenza is shown as the share of tested samples that were positive, because laboratory detections are not counts of people ill.
methodology.defaults.title: Which series is shown by default
methodology.defaults.p1: Each disease has one default series, set in the disease configuration: influenza uses WHO FluNet laboratory detections summed over surveillance systems; COVID-19 uses WHO confirmed cases; mpox uses WHO confirmed cases; measles uses WHO’s provisional monthly total; cholera uses annual reported cases processed by Our World in Data from WHO; polio uses WHO’s annual officially reported cases; dengue uses a yearly series built from OpenDengue.
methodology.defaults.p2: The rule is: prefer the primary official publisher, then the finest time resolution it offers with national coverage. Other series stay available in Analyst mode and are never blended into the default.
methodology.aggregation.title: Aggregation
methodology.aggregation.p1: Daily values are summed into ISO weeks and an unfinished last week is dropped. Global totals add up only the countries that reported in each period, so the set of countries changes over time. Missing periods are never treated as zero.
methodology.revisions.title: Revision history (data vintage)
methodology.revisions.p1: Every pipeline run compares each value with the previous snapshot and stores only what is new, changed or removed. From this, the site can rebuild exactly what it showed at any earlier snapshot. Snapshot ids are permanent.
methodology.revisions.p2: Vintage reflects what this site retrieved and published, not necessarily when a source first released a number.
methodology.lag.title: Reporting lag and incomplete periods
methodology.lag.p1: For each source, the lag is the age (in periods) by which 90% of meaningful revisions have happened, estimated from the stored revisions. Until at least four snapshots and thirty revised values exist, a configured default is used and labelled as such.
methodology.lag.p2: The most recent periods within that lag are marked “likely incomplete”, shaded on charts, and excluded from trend arrows, percentage changes, map windows and signal flags.
methodology.reconcile.title: When sources disagree
methodology.reconcile.p1: Where two sources report the same disease, place, period, metric and case definition, both are shown side by side. They are flagged as disagreeing when they differ by more than 5 and by more than 5% of the larger value. Nothing is averaged or merged.
methodology.flags.title: Automated signal flags
methodology.flags.p1: For each country’s default weekly or monthly series, a period is flagged when its count exceeds the mean of seven baseline periods (ending three periods earlier) by more than three standard deviations, is at least twice that mean, and is at least 20 (weekly) or 30 (monthly). The standard deviation is never taken below the square root of the mean, which protects low counts.
methodology.flags.p2: Periods marked likely incomplete are never flagged. Holiday weeks (ISO weeks 52, 53 and 1) and counts that follow a missing or zero period (a sign of batch reporting) are not flagged. For seasonal diseases the count must also exceed the usual range for that time of year in earlier years.
methodology.flags.p3: Flags produce false positives (reporting changes, testing drives, backlogs) and miss real changes. They are labels on a page, not alerts.
methodology.events.title: Event notices
methodology.events.p1: Events come from WHO Disease Outbreak News and US CDC travel health notices. Disease names are matched against a mapping table; unmatched names appear under “Other / unclassified” and are reported to maintainers rather than guessed. Notices about the same disease and overlapping places, no more than 120 days apart, are grouped into one event.
methodology.events.p2: Case and death counts are read from the notice text by pattern matching and always shown with the exact quoted phrase. Status uses “ongoing” or “declared over” only when the notice says so; after 90 days without a notice an event shows “no recent update”, which is a recency indicator and not a judgment.
methodology.geocoding.title: Locations and precision
methodology.geocoding.p1: Locations are derived offline from the project’s own tables (Natural Earth country shapes, GeoNames regions and cities). Countries are taken from the notice title. A region or city is added only when its name appears next to an administrative word such as “Province” or “city of”.
methodology.geocoding.p2: Every location carries its precision: country, first-level region, second-level district or named city. A country-level point is the middle of the country, not the place where cases occurred. No second-level gazetteer is bundled yet, so that level is not produced.
methodology.ranking.title: List order of outbreaks
methodology.ranking.p1: The order score is 0.45 × recency + 0.25 × cases + 0.10 × deaths + 0.10 × countries + 0.10 × source type, where recency decays with days since the last notice, counts are on a capped logarithmic scale, and source type is 1.0 for WHO Disease Outbreak News and 0.6 for travel notices. It orders a list; it does not rate severity.
methodology.transforms.title: Workbench transforms
methodology.transforms.p1: Transforms are applied in a fixed order: per-capita, rolling average, cumulative, percent of peak, align by first report. Rolling averages are trailing and blank wherever a period in the window is missing. Active transforms appear in the chart subtitle and in every export.
methodology.simulation.title: Simulation engine
methodology.simulation.p1: The sandbox runs standard compartmental, stochastic, network and metapopulation models from a declarative model specification. Solvers are tested against analytical results and recorded reference outputs. See the simulation documentation for the model catalogue, equations and validation.
methodology.simulation.p2: The engine has no access to the reported data. There is no fitting, calibration, reproduction-number estimation, nowcasting or forecasting anywhere on this site.
methodology.quality.title: Validation and failures
methodology.quality.p1: Each fetched file is checked for schema, date range and plausibility against the previous snapshot. Suspicious output, such as many values dropping to zero or a flood of new events, is quarantined: the last good data stays live and a public issue is opened for a person to review. The pipeline never repairs itself.
methodology.limits.title: Limitations
methodology.limits.p1: Reported cases undercount infections, by an amount that differs by disease, place and time. Annual series (cholera, polio, dengue) say nothing about the current year. Dengue definitions differ between countries. No sub-national series are included. The reporting-lag estimates start from defaults and improve only as snapshots accumulate.
methodology.compare.title: Do not compare counts across diseases
methodology.compare.p1: Each disease is counted by a different surveillance system with a different case definition. A count of laboratory detections of influenza, confirmed COVID-19 cases and notified measles cases are different kinds of number. Compare a disease with itself over time, or places with each other within one disease and definition, preferably per 100,000 people.
about.what.title: What this is
about.what.p1: An open-source website that gathers official public reports about infectious diseases, shows them on maps and charts, explains how to read them, and lets anyone trace each number back to its original publication.
about.not.title: What this is not
about.not.p1: It is not a surveillance system, not an early-warning service, not a forecasting service and not medical advice. It has no monitoring authority. Automated flags and simulations are explanatory tools, never alerts, predictions or judgments.
about.audiences.title: Who it is for
about.audiences.p1: People following disease activity, journalists who need accurate numbers with sources, and researchers who need citable, versioned data. Simple mode explains; Analyst mode shows the same numbers with more detail.
about.trust.title: How trust is built in
about.trust.p1: Every item shows its source and “data as of” date. Missing data looks missing. Recent periods are marked as incomplete. Disagreements between sources are shown, not hidden. Corrections are logged publicly.
about.open.title: Open source
about.open.p1: Code is under the MIT license and written content under CC BY 4.0. Data keeps each source’s own license, which is carried into every export with a suggested citation.
about.privacy.title: Privacy
about.privacy.p1: There is no tracking, no analytics, no accounts and no cookies. Your browser only requests this site’s own files. Data you load into the workbench stays in your browser and is never uploaded.
about.languages.title: Languages
about.languages.p1: English is the source language. Spanish, French and German were drafted by machine and are awaiting human review; health-related wording is the priority. Titles and text from sources are shown in their original language with a link.
glossary.case-definition.def: The rules a health system uses to decide what counts as a case. Different definitions give different numbers for the same outbreak.
glossary.confirmed.def: A case confirmed by a laboratory test, or by the confirmation rule the source uses.
glossary.probable.def: A case that meets clinical criteria and has a link to a confirmed case or a supportive test, but no confirming test.
glossary.suspected.def: A person with symptoms that fit the disease, before or without testing.
glossary.notified.def: A case officially reported to health authorities under whatever definition that country uses.
glossary.incidence.def: New cases in a period, often given per 100,000 people.
glossary.per-capita.def: A count divided by population, so that places of different size can be compared.
glossary.reporting-lag.def: The delay between someone falling ill and their case appearing in published numbers.
glossary.incomplete.def: Recent periods for which reports are probably still arriving. Their numbers usually rise later.
glossary.revision.def: A change a source makes to a number it published earlier.
glossary.snapshot.def: A fixed, permanent record of everything this site published at one moment.
glossary.undercounting.def: Reported cases are fewer than true infections, because not everyone is tested, diagnosed or reported.
glossary.surveillance.def: The way a health system collects case information, for example from all clinics or from a sample of sites.
glossary.sentinel.def: Collecting detailed data from a chosen set of sites rather than from everywhere.
glossary.percent-positive.def: The share of tested samples that were positive. It depends on who gets tested.
glossary.epi-curve.def: A chart of new cases per period, used to see how an outbreak grows and declines.
glossary.rolling-average.def: The average of the last few periods, used to smooth irregular reporting.
glossary.log-scale.def: An axis where each step multiplies the value by ten, so steady percentage growth looks like a straight line.
glossary.signal-flag.def: An automatic, informational note that a reported count is unusually high for that place. It is not an alert.
glossary.baseline.def: The recent periods a new value is compared against.
glossary.origin-type.def: Whether an item was reported by a source, computed by this site, supplied by you, or simulated.
glossary.lineage.def: The full path of a number: the raw file, where it sits in that file, and every step applied to it.
glossary.r0.def: In a model, the average number of people one infected person infects when nobody is immune. It depends on behaviour and setting, not only on the pathogen.
glossary.r0.src: Delamater PL et al. Complexity of the basic reproduction number (R0). Emerging Infectious Diseases 2019;25(1):1–4. doi:10.3201/eid2501.171901 (bibliographic record checked against Crossref on 2026-11-10)
glossary.herd-immunity.def: In a simple model, the share of people who must be immune for an infection to stop growing: 1 − 1/R0.
glossary.simulation.def: A calculation of what a simplified model does under chosen assumptions. On this site it is for learning, never a forecast.
guide.percapita.title: Per-capita versus raw counts
guide.percapita.p1: Raw counts mostly tell you which countries are large. To compare places, use cases per 100,000 people. To describe the burden in one place, the raw count is fine. Say which one you are using.
guide.lag.title: Reporting lag
guide.lag.p1: The latest weeks almost always look lower than they will once late reports arrive. Do not write that cases are falling on the strength of the most recent, shaded periods. Compare complete periods.
guide.undercount.title: Undercounting
guide.undercount.p1: Reported cases are the cases that were tested, diagnosed and reported. Write “reported cases” or “confirmed cases”, not “cases” or “infections”, and avoid implying that the reported number is the total.
guide.compare.title: Comparing countries
guide.compare.p1: Differences between countries reflect testing, access to care and reporting rules as well as disease. A country that looks worse may simply be looking harder. Check that the case definition is the same before comparing.
guide.definitions.title: Case definitions
guide.definitions.p1: Suspected, probable and confirmed cases are different numbers. A switch from one definition to another can look like a sudden rise or fall. The source chip on each chart shows which definition is used.
guide.uncertainty.title: Describing uncertainty
guide.uncertainty.p1: Give the date the data was retrieved and say that numbers may be revised. Prefer “at least” for counts. When sources disagree, say so and name both.
guide.simulations.title: Describing simulations
guide.simulations.p1: Outputs from “Learn and simulate” illustrate how a simplified model behaves. They are not fitted to real data. Never present them as predictions, projections or estimates for a real place, and keep the “illustrative simulation” label on any image.
guide.trace.title: Tracing and citing a number
guide.trace.p1: Click the source chip next to any chart, map or number to open “Trace this”. It shows the original source link, the date it was retrieved, the license and what was done to the data. Cite the original source and say you obtained it via this site.
guide.cite.title: Citing this site responsibly
guide.cite.p1: Use a snapshot-pinned link so readers see exactly what you saw. Do not describe this site as a monitoring or alert system. Automated flags are statistical notes, not findings.
tour.epicurve.title: How to read an epi-curve
tour.epicurve.s1: This chart shows how many cases were reported in each period. Time runs left to right; the height is the reported count.
tour.epicurve.s2: A rising line means more cases were reported than the period before. It does not tell you how many people were infected, only how many were counted.
tour.epicurve.s3: The subtitle tells you what has been done to the numbers, for example “per 100,000 people”. “As reported” means nothing was changed.
tour.epicurve.s4: The legend names each line. Dashed lines are simulated or user-supplied and are never official data.
tour.recentlow.title: Why recent weeks look low
tour.recentlow.s1: The hatched area marks the most recent periods. Reports for these are still arriving, so the numbers are too low for now.
tour.recentlow.s2: This note explains that those periods are left out of trends and percentage changes. A dip inside the hatched area is not a real decline.
tour.recentlow.s3: You can hide the likely-incomplete periods altogether with this option.
tour.recentlow.s4: To see why this happens, open the “why reported data lags” lesson in Learn and simulate, which shows a true epidemic next to its delayed reports.
tour.percapita.title: What per-capita changes
tour.percapita.s1: Tick “Per 100,000 people” to divide each count by the country’s population.
tour.percapita.s2: Large countries usually drop and small countries rise. The ranking by raw count mostly reflects population size.
tour.percapita.s3: The subtitle now records the transform, and so will any image or download you make.
tour.definitions.title: How case definitions differ
tour.definitions.s1: The source chip names the source and the kind of data. Open it to see the case definition in use.
tour.definitions.s2: When a chart mixes definitions or sources, a warning appears here with a button to restrict the chart to comparable data.
tour.definitions.s3: Each line in the legend is one source or definition. They are shown side by side and never added together.
tour.flag.title: How to read a signal flag
tour.flag.s1: A flag means a reported count was well above that place’s own recent baseline. It is produced by a simple formula.
tour.flag.s2: In Analyst mode you can see the value, the baseline mean, the threshold and the baseline window that triggered it.
tour.flag.s3: Flags can be caused by a backlog being reported at once, more testing or a change of definition. They are notes, not alerts.
tour.flag.s4: Periods marked likely incomplete are never flagged, and many real changes are never flagged.
tour.trace.title: How to trace a number to its source
tour.trace.s1: Every chart, map and list has a source chip like this one. It shows the origin type, the source name and the “data as of” date.
tour.trace.s2: Click it to open “Trace this”: the original source link, when it was retrieved, the license and each step applied. One more click shows the full lineage, down to the raw file hash.
tour.trace.s3: Images, downloads and embeds made from these buttons carry the same source information with them.

assume.fails: known to fail in real outbreaks
assume.homogeneousMixing: Everyone is equally likely to meet everyone else.
assume.homogeneousMixing.why: Real contact happens in households, schools, workplaces and networks, which changes speed and final size.
assume.mixingByGroup: People mix evenly within each age group, at fixed rates between groups.
assume.mixingByGroup.why: Real contact patterns vary by place, day and behaviour, and the matrix here is invented.
assume.constantRates: Transmission and recovery rates stay the same over time.
assume.constantRates.why: Behaviour, weather, new variants and policy change them.
assume.seasonalRates: Transmission follows a smooth yearly cycle.
assume.seasonalRates.why: Real seasonality is irregular and differs by place.
assume.closedPopulation: Nobody enters or leaves the population.
assume.closedPopulation.why: People are born, die, travel and move.
assume.openPopulation: Births and deaths happen at constant, equal rates.
assume.exponentialDurations: Each stage lasts a random time whose most likely value is zero (exponential waiting times).
assume.exponentialDurations.why: Real incubation and infectious periods cluster around a typical length. Use more stages for a more realistic shape.
assume.erlangDurations: Stage durations cluster around their average (several sub-stages).
assume.noBehaviourChange: People do not change behaviour in response to the outbreak.
assume.noBehaviourChange.why: People usually do, which changes the curve in ways this model cannot show.
assume.perfectObservation: The model shows true infections, as if every one were seen instantly.
assume.perfectObservation.why: Real data is delayed and incomplete. Open the observation layer to see the difference.
assume.deterministic: The outcome is fully determined: no chance.
assume.deterministic.why: With few cases, chance decides whether an outbreak takes off at all.
assume.stochastic: Chance events are simulated; each run is one of many possible outcomes.
assume.lifelongImmunity: Recovered people stay immune for the whole simulation.
assume.lifelongImmunity.why: For many infections immunity wanes or new variants escape it.

lesson.exponential-growth.title: Exponential growth and doubling time
lesson.exponential-growth.sum: why small numbers become large ones quickly
lesson.exponential-growth.p1: Early in an outbreak each infected person infects more than one other, so the number of infected people multiplies by a fixed factor in each period. That is exponential growth.
lesson.exponential-growth.p2: A useful way to describe it is the doubling time: how long it takes for the number of infected people to double. A short doubling time means little time to react.
lesson.exponential-growth.try: Run the model, then raise R0 and watch the early doubling time shrink. Switch the main chart to see how long the curve looks flat before it suddenly rises.
lesson.exponential-growth.take: Exponential growth looks like nothing is happening, and then like everything is happening at once. It always slows eventually, because susceptible people run out.
lesson.r0.title: What R0 really means
lesson.r0.sum: and why it is not a fixed property of a disease
lesson.r0.p1: R0 is the average number of people one infected person would infect in a population where nobody is immune. If it is above 1 an outbreak can grow; below 1 it dies out.
lesson.r0.p2: R0 is not a constant of nature. It is the product of how infectious the pathogen is, how often people meet, and how long they are infectious. Change behaviour or setting and R0 changes, which is why published estimates for the same disease differ widely.
lesson.r0.try: Keep R0 fixed and change the infectious period: the curve changes speed although R0 is the same. Then reduce contacts and watch the reproduction number at the start fall.
lesson.r0.take: R0 describes a pathogen in a particular population at a particular time. The same R0 can go with fast or slow outbreaks.
lesson.herd-immunity.title: Herd immunity and vaccination thresholds
lesson.herd-immunity.sum: why real thresholds differ from the simple formula
lesson.herd-immunity.p1: If enough people are immune, each infected person infects fewer than one other on average and outbreaks cannot grow. In the simplest model that share is 1 − 1/R0.
lesson.herd-immunity.p2: Vaccines are not perfect, so coverage must be higher than the threshold: divide by efficacy. A vaccine that fully protects some people behaves differently from one that partly protects everyone. And real populations do not mix evenly, so clusters of unvaccinated people can sustain outbreaks even when average coverage is high.
lesson.herd-immunity.try: Find the lowest coverage that stops the outbreak. Lower the efficacy and find it again. Then switch between the two vaccine types.
lesson.herd-immunity.take: The formula 1 − 1/R0 is a starting point from an idealised model, not a target for a real population.
lesson.flattening.title: Flattening the curve, and overshoot
lesson.flattening.sum: what temporary measures do and do not change
lesson.flattening.p1: Reducing contacts lowers the peak and delays it. If the measures end while many people are still susceptible, the epidemic can resume.
lesson.flattening.p2: An uncontrolled epidemic overshoots: it keeps infecting people after the herd immunity threshold is passed, because many people are infectious at that moment. A well-timed reduction can cut that overshoot and so reduce the total number infected, not only the peak.
lesson.flattening.try: Pin the run without intervention, then add a contact reduction. Move its start and end days and compare the peak and the final size.
lesson.flattening.take: Timing matters as much as strength. Measures that end too early delay infections without preventing them.
lesson.epidemics-end.title: Why epidemics end before everyone is infected
lesson.epidemics-end.sum: the final size of an epidemic
lesson.epidemics-end.p1: As people recover and become immune, each infected person meets fewer susceptible people. Once the effective reproduction number falls below 1 the epidemic shrinks, although susceptible people remain.
lesson.epidemics-end.p2: In the simplest model the share finally infected follows a formula that depends only on R0. For R0 = 2 about 80% are infected, not 100%.
lesson.epidemics-end.try: Look at the final-size readout and the effective reproduction number chart. Raise R0 step by step and note how the final size changes.
lesson.epidemics-end.take: An epidemic ends when infections cannot find enough susceptible people, not when everyone has been infected.
lesson.fade-out.title: Chance and stochastic fade-out
lesson.fade-out.sum: why some introductions never take off
lesson.fade-out.p1: When only a few people are infected, chance decides a great deal. The first cases may happen not to infect anyone, and the outbreak ends before it starts.
lesson.fade-out.p2: Smooth model curves hide this. Running the same model many times with random events shows the range of outcomes, including early extinction.
lesson.fade-out.try: Run the ensemble with one or two initial cases and R0 just above 1. Then increase the initial cases and see the extinction probability fall.
lesson.fade-out.take: An R0 above 1 means an outbreak can grow, not that every introduction will.
lesson.superspreading.title: Superspreading
lesson.superspreading.sum: when a few cases cause most transmission
lesson.superspreading.p1: The average number of secondary cases hides large differences between individuals. For some infections most cases infect nobody and a few infect many.
lesson.superspreading.p2: This variation is described by a dispersion parameter, k. Small k means strong superspreading: introductions usually die out, but the ones that survive grow explosively.
lesson.superspreading.try: Keep R at 1.5 and lower k. Watch the chance of extinction rise and the share of transmission from the top 20% grow.
lesson.superspreading.take: The same average can describe very different epidemics. Averages alone do not tell you how an outbreak will start.
lesson.seasonality.title: Seasonality
lesson.seasonality.sum: why some infections return every year
lesson.seasonality.p1: If transmission is a little higher in one season, and immunity fades or new susceptible people arrive, an infection can return in regular waves.
lesson.seasonality.p2: Small seasonal changes in transmission can produce large waves, because they act on exponential growth. The timing of waves depends on immunity as well as weather.
lesson.seasonality.try: Raise the seasonal swing from zero and watch regular waves appear. Change how long immunity lasts and see the pattern shift.
lesson.seasonality.take: Seasonal patterns come from the interplay of transmission, immunity and susceptible people, not from weather alone.
lesson.vaccine-waning.title: Vaccination and waning immunity
lesson.vaccine-waning.sum: why protection can erode over time
lesson.vaccine-waning.p1: If vaccine protection fades, a population that was above the herd immunity threshold drifts back below it. An outbreak that was impossible becomes possible again.
lesson.vaccine-waning.p2: This is why some vaccines need boosters, and why a single coverage figure does not describe protection for long.
lesson.vaccine-waning.try: Start with high coverage and lasting protection: no outbreak. Now shorten the duration of vaccine protection and extend the simulated time.
lesson.vaccine-waning.take: Coverage and duration of protection have to be considered together.
lesson.reporting-lag.title: Why reported data lags and undercounts
lesson.reporting-lag.p1: Reported cases are not infections. Between an infection and a number on a chart there are symptoms, a decision to seek care, a test, a result, a report and a publication. Each step loses some cases and adds delay.
lesson.reporting-lag.p2: As a result, reported curves are lower and later than the true epidemic, and the most recent days always look too low because their reports have not arrived yet.
lesson.reporting-lag.try: Open the panel “From the true epidemic to reported data” below the chart. Press “Set today to the true peak” and compare the two curves at the right-hand edge.
lesson.reporting-lag.take: A drop at the end of a reported curve is usually missing reports, not falling infections. That is why this site shades recent periods and leaves them out of trends.
lesson.limits.title: The limits of every model
lesson.limits.p1: Every model is a simplification. The models here assume even mixing, fixed rates and no change in behaviour, and they know nothing about any real place.
lesson.limits.p2: Models are useful for understanding mechanisms: why curves have the shape they do, what an intervention can and cannot change. They become predictions only with careful fitting to good data, expert judgment and honest uncertainty, none of which this site provides.
lesson.limits.try: Open “Model documentation” under the chart and read the assumptions panel. For each assumption, ask how a real outbreak would differ.
lesson.limits.take: Use these simulations to ask better questions about the reported data, never to answer them.
mis.lead: Ideas that are often repeated, and what the models and the data actually show.
mis.r0-fixed.fix: R0 depends on contact patterns and setting as well as the pathogen. Published values for one disease span a wide range.
mis.herd-formula.claim: Herd immunity is reached at exactly 1 − 1/R0.
mis.herd-formula.fix: That is the result for an idealised, evenly mixed population with a perfect vaccine. Imperfect vaccines, waning and uneven coverage all change it.
mis.everyone-infected.fix: Epidemics end when too few susceptible people remain to sustain them, which happens before everyone is infected.
mis.flatten-reduces-total.claim: Flattening the curve always reduces the total number infected.
mis.flatten-reduces-total.fix: It lowers and delays the peak. Whether it reduces the total depends on timing and on what happens when measures end.
mis.model-is-forecast.claim: A model curve shows what will happen.
mis.model-is-forecast.fix: A curve shows what a set of assumptions implies. The simulations here are not fitted to any data and predict nothing.
mis.reported-is-true.claim: Reported cases are the number of infections.
mis.reported-is-true.fix: Reported cases are the infections that were tested, diagnosed and reported. The true number is higher, by an amount that varies.
mis.recent-drop.claim: The latest numbers are lower, so the outbreak is declining.
mis.recent-drop.fix: The latest periods are incomplete because reports arrive late. Wait for them to fill in before reading a trend.
mis.superspreaders-rare.claim: Every infected person infects about R others.
mis.superspreaders-rare.fix: R is an average. For many infections most people infect nobody and a few infect many.
notpred.p1: Everything in “Learn and simulate” is a teaching tool. A simulation shows what follows from a set of simplifying assumptions. It is not a statement about the world.
notpred.li1: No model is fitted, calibrated or tuned to the reported data shown elsewhere on the site.
notpred.li2: No simulation starts from current reported counts, and none is drawn on future calendar dates. Time is counted in days from an arbitrary start.
notpred.li3: Settings are invented: “a town of 10,000”, not a real place. Disease-flavoured presets are illustrative ranges, with their sources shown.
notpred.li4: There is no estimation of reproduction numbers from real data, no nowcasting and no forecasting.
notpred.li5: Simulated lines are dashed, purple and labelled SIMULATED, and are never drawn on the same axis as reported data.
notpred.li6: A simulated curve that resembles a past outbreak proves nothing: many different models can produce similar shapes.
notpred.end.p1: Real forecasting needs models fitted to carefully understood data, with uncertainty stated and results checked against what later happened. That work is done by public health agencies and research groups. It is outside the scope of this site.
notpred.end.p2: If you publish an image from the sandbox, keep its “illustrative simulation” label and describe it as a simulation.
challenge.lead: Puzzles about how a model behaves. They are exercises in reasoning about the model, not advice about policy.
challenge.puzzle: This is a puzzle about a simplified model. Real decisions involve far more than a curve.
challenge.capacity.title: Stay under the line
challenge.capacity.goal: Keep the peak of infectious people below the capacity line of 600, using only a contact reduction that starts on day 20. Choose its strength and its end day.
challenge.capacity.why: A moderate reduction held long enough works better than a strong one that ends early, which only postpones the peak.
challenge.coverage.title: Just enough vaccine
challenge.coverage.goal: With R0 = 4 and a vaccine that is 90% effective, prevent an outbreak (fewer than 2% infected) with the lowest coverage you can.
challenge.coverage.why: The threshold is (1 − 1/R0) divided by efficacy, about 83% here. Going far above it adds little in this model.
challenge.overshoot.title: Cut the overshoot
challenge.overshoot.goal: You have one 30-day period in which contacts are halved. Choose when it starts so that fewer than 80% of people are infected in total.
challenge.overshoot.why: Acting around the peak removes the overshoot. Acting very early only delays the same epidemic.
refs.lead: Sources behind the presets and methods in this section. Each shows whether it has been checked against the source.
refs.matricesBody: No contact-survey data is bundled, because no openly licensed source was verified for this build. The age-structured model uses a synthetic matrix that you can edit.
teach.lead: Ready-made scenarios for a class or workshop. Each opens in the sandbox, has a printable worksheet, and can be shared as a link. No accounts are needed.
teach.noAccounts: Nothing is stored on a server. Scenarios live in the link itself.
scenario.town-outbreak.title: An outbreak in a town of 10,000
scenario.town-outbreak.setup: Five people are infectious in a town of 10,000. Each infects 2.5 others on average while infectious for 5 days.
scenario.town-outbreak.q1: Before running the model, sketch how you expect the number of infectious people to change over 160 days.
scenario.town-outbreak.q2: Run the model. On which day is the peak, and how many people are infectious then?
scenario.town-outbreak.q3: What share of the town is infected by the end? Why is it not 100%?
scenario.town-outbreak.q4: Halve the infectious period. What changes, and what stays the same?
scenario.school-outbreak.title: An outbreak in a school of 800
scenario.school-outbreak.setup: One person is infectious in a school of 800. There is a 2-day incubation period before people become infectious.
scenario.school-outbreak.q1: How does the incubation period change the early part of the curve compared with the town scenario?
scenario.school-outbreak.q2: Switch to a stochastic solver and run it five times with different seeds. How many runs produce a large outbreak?
scenario.school-outbreak.q3: Why do some runs die out although R0 is 3?
scenario.school-outbreak.q4: Name two things about a real school that this model leaves out.
scenario.below-threshold.title: Below the threshold
scenario.below-threshold.setup: Fifty people are infectious, but each infects only 0.9 others on average.
scenario.below-threshold.q1: Predict what happens to the number of infectious people.
scenario.below-threshold.q2: Run the model. How many people are infected in total?
scenario.below-threshold.q3: Raise R0 slowly. At what value does the behaviour change?
scenario.below-threshold.q4: Explain in one sentence what the threshold at R0 = 1 means.
scenario.vaccinate-town.title: Vaccinating a town
scenario.vaccinate-town.setup: R0 is 4. Sixty percent of people were vaccinated before the outbreak with a vaccine that is 90% effective.
scenario.vaccinate-town.q1: Is 60% coverage enough to prevent an outbreak? Predict, then run.
scenario.vaccinate-town.q2: Find the lowest coverage that prevents an outbreak.
scenario.vaccinate-town.q3: Compare your answer with 1 − 1/R0. Why is it higher?
scenario.vaccinate-town.q4: Switch the vaccine type to “leaky”. What changes?
scenario.flatten.title: Flattening the curve
scenario.flatten.setup: Contacts are reduced by 45% from day 20 to day 80.
scenario.flatten.q1: Pin a run without the intervention, then compare. What happens to the peak?
scenario.flatten.q3: Move the start day earlier and later. When does the intervention reduce the final size most?
scenario.flatten.q4: What would have to be true in reality for this result to hold?
scenario.waning.title: When immunity fades
scenario.waning.setup: Immunity lasts 200 days on average, after which people become susceptible again.
scenario.waning.q1: Predict the shape of the curve over 1,000 days.
scenario.waning.q2: Run the model. What does the number of infectious people settle to?
scenario.waning.q3: Make immunity last longer. How do the waves change?
scenario.waning.q4: Which real infections behave more like this model than like the SIR model?
tool.basic.desc: Choose a model, move the sliders, and see the epidemic curve, the key numbers and the model’s equations update.
tool.ensemble.desc: Run hundreds of seeded random realisations and see the range of outcomes, the chance of early extinction, and whether enough runs were done.
tool.branching.desc: Compare Poisson and negative-binomial offspring distributions and see how dispersion changes the chance of extinction.
tool.ngm.desc: Compute the reproduction number of a model with several infected groups, with the matrices shown.
tool.sweeps.desc: One- and two-way sweeps, Latin hypercube sampling, partial rank correlations and a tornado table.
tool.phase.desc: See equilibria and their stability for models with an endemic state.
tool.network.desc: Spread on random, small-world, scale-free and community networks, compared with even mixing.
tool.metapop.desc: Place illustrative patches on the map and link them with a synthetic mobility rule.
tool.builder.desc: Add compartments and flows, write rate expressions from a safe list, and see the equations and checks.

mappage.means.missing: Dotted areas report to this source but have not yet reported for this period. Hatched areas have no report for it. Neither pattern means there is no disease.
